title: Scan Others for Clues About You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership takes Franklin's line about steel, diamonds and self-knowledge as the setup for a practical problem: self-contemplation alone cannot deliver an accurate picture of oneself, and the obvious remedy, asking for feedback, is compromised at the source. The piece argues that solicited feedback is only as good as the candour of the person giving it, and that people are systematically reluctant to tell a leader what they actually think, particularly when they will have to absorb the reaction. Rather than proposing better feedback mechanics, the essay names a quieter alternative: sustained observation of how others behave around you. The distinction it draws is between perceptions, which people can hide, and reactions, which they cannot. The prescription is deliberately mundane and continuous, a running set of questions about how people look at you, what they say, when they go quiet, backed by note-taking. It closes with Feynman on self-deception, which frames the whole exercise as a defence against the easiest error to make.
points: The core claim is that solicited feedback is bounded by the honesty of the giver, so the usable signal about how a leader lands comes from watching reactions rather than collecting opinions.
The operative distinction is between perception and reaction: people can and do conceal what they think of you, but they are poor at controlling how they visibly respond to you.
The practice is framed as continuous rather than episodic, a daily scan of how people look at you, address you, respond to you and fall silent around you, with notes kept.
Asking for feedback is treated as a first step requiring courage, not a solution, and the piece is explicit that hiring a third party is the only way to buy materially more candour.
Feynman's line about being the easiest person to fool positions self-knowledge as an active defence, not a reflective luxury.
quotes: Really knowing yourself requires genuine insight and often takes years to do.
Knowing the many facets of yourself is a critical pursuit. And self contemplation only goes so far.
The truth is, people don’t like to tell us what they really think.
The best leaders know the secret step in this process — observation.
By watching how others respond to what we say and do, we cut through the red tape of getting candid feedback.
People may hide their perceptions, but they are lousy at masking their reactions.
